E010-01.notes: Participle 'facing' takes its object directly; no punctuation between verb and object. A/B/D all insert illegal punctuation.

E010-02.notes: Plural 'they' needs 'were'; past time ('Built in the 1920s and 1930s') rules out 'is' and 'has been' (also singular).

E010-03.notes: Only A states the purpose (early warning of aircraft); B-D concern durability/cost/material, which do not explain why they were built.

E010-04.notes: 'where a listener ... could detect' is a restrictive/relative clause; no comma after 'where' (A), no semicolon (B, not an independent clause before it... and fragment after), and C splits subject 'a listener with a microphone' from its verb.

E010-05.notes: Contrast between 'when conditions were ideal' and 'conditions were rarely ideal' requires 'However'.

E010-06.notes: Compound subject 'Wind, waves, and the noise' is plural, ruling out 'was', 'drowns', 'has'; simple past matches 'shrank' and the narrative. Trap: nearest noun 'boats'/'noise' and 'was' sounding natural.

E010-07.notes: The sentence says radar made the mirrors obsolete. A and B describe content found elsewhere; C (satellites) is not in the passage.

E010-08.notes: Two independent clauses; semicolon fixes the comma splice. B is fused; D is still a splice with an extra comma.

E010-09.notes: Pronoun is the subject of 'stands' inside the noun clause, so 'whoever', even though the clause is object of 'by'. 'whom'/'whomever' trap catches many; 'whichever' is for things/choices.

flags: minor: D echoes the exact phrase 'experiment in hearing' from paragraph 1, making it easy to match on the surface; 'A century later' is approximately right (1920s-30s to the present).
E010-10.notes: Only D ties back to the opening ('experiment in hearing') and to the preceding whisper demonstration; A is irrelevant, B and C drift off topic.

E010-11.notes: Essay explains how the mirrors worked and that radar made them obsolete. B overstates radar detail; C misstates the focus; D is false.

passage_flags: minor: Opening says the structures stand on a shingle beach 'near the English coast'; a beach is the coast, so 'on the English coast' would be cleaner (the real Denge mirrors sit in a gravel/lake area at Greatstone near Dungeness).

Historical details (1920s-1930s construction, ~60 m wall plus two dishes, ~20-mile ideal range, made obsolete by radar in the late 1930s, occasional guided open days) are consistent with the Denge sound mirrors; no factual problems found.
